paragraphs: U.S. customers historically tipped people they assumed were earning most of their income via tips, such as restaurant servers earning less than the minimum wage. In the early 2010s, a wide range of businesses started processing purchases with iPads and other digital payment systems. These systems often prompted customers to tip for services that were not previously tipped.

Today's tip requests are often not connected to the salary and service norms that used to determine when and how people tip. Customers in the past nearly always paid tips after receiving a service, such as at the conclusion of a restaurant meal, after getting a haircut or once a pizza was delivered. That timing could reward high-quality service and give workers an incentive to provide it.
It's becoming more common for tips to be requested beforehand. And new tipping technology may even automatically add tips.

The prevalence of digital payment devices has made it easier to ask customers for a tip. That helps explain why tip requests are creeping into new kinds of services. Customers now routinely see menus of suggested default options — often well above 20% of what they owe. The amounts have risen from 10% or less in the 1950s to 15% around the year 2000 to 20% or higher today. This increase is sometimes called tipflation — the expectation of ever-higher tip amounts.

Tipping has always been a vital source of income for workers in historically tipped services, like restaurants, where the tipped minimum wage can be as low as US$2.13 an hour. Tip creep and tipflation are now further supplementing the income of many low-wage service workers.

Notably, tipping primarily benefits some of these workers, such as waiters, but not others, such as cooks and dishwashers. To ensure that all employees were paid fair wages, some restaurants banned tipping and increased prices, but this movement toward no-tipping services has largely fizzled out.

So, to increase employee wages without raising prices, more employers are succumbing to the temptations of tip creep and tipflation. However, many customers are frustrated because they feel they are being asked for too high of a tip, too often. And, as our research emphasizes, tipping now seems to be more coercive, less generous and often completely dissociated from service quality.

paragraphs: When it was established, the National Health Service (NHS) was visionary: offering high-quality, timely care to meet the dominant needs of the population it served. Nearly 75 years on, with the UK facing very different health challenges, it is clear that model is out of date.

From life expectancy to cancer and infant mortality rates, we are lagging behind many of our peers. With more than 6.8 million on waitlists, healthcare is becoming increasingly inaccessible for those who cannot opt to pay for private treatment; and the cost of providing healthcare is increasingly squeezing out investment in other public services. As demand for healthcare continues to grow, pressures on the workforce — which is already near breaking point — will only become more acute.

Many of the answers to the crisis in health and care are well rehearsed. We need to be much better at reducing and diverting demand on health services, rather than simply managing it. Much more needs to be invested in communities and primary care to reduce our reliance on hospitals. And capacity in social care needs to be greater, to support the growing number of people living with long-term conditions.

Yet despite two decades of strategies and a number of major health reforms, we have failed to make meaningful progress on any of these aims. That is why the Reform think tank is launching a new programme of work entitled "Reimagining health", supported by ten former health ministers. Together, we are calling for a much more open and honest conversation about the future of health in the UK, and an "urgent rethink" of the hospital-centric model we retain.

This must begin with the question of how we maximise the health of the nation, rather than "fix" the NHS. It is estimated, for example, that healthcare accounts for only about 20% of health outcomes. Much more important are the places we live, work and socialise — yet there is no clear cross-government strategy for improving these social determinants of health. Worse, when policies like the national obesity strategy are scrapped, taxpayers are left with the heavy price tag of treating the illnesses, like diabetes, that result.

Reform wants to ask how power and resources should be distributed in our health system. What health functions should remain at the centre, and what should be given to local leaders, often responsible for services that create health, and with a much better understanding of the needs of their populations?

paragraphs: Heat action plans, or HAPs, have been proliferating in India in the past few years. In general, an HAP spells out when and how officials should issue heat warnings and alert hospitals and other institutions. Nagpur's plan, for instance, calls for hospitals to set aside "cold wards" in the summer for treating heatstroke patients, and advises builders to give construction laborers a break from work on very hot days.

But implementation of existing HAPs has been uneven, according to a report from the Centre for Policy Research. Many lack adequate funding, it found. And their triggering thresholds often are not customized to the local climate. In some areas, high daytime temperatures alone might serve as an adequate trigger for alerts. But in other places, nighttime temperatures or humidity might be as important a gauge of risk as daytime highs.

Mumbai's April heatstroke deaths highlighted the need for more nuanced and localized warnings, researchers say. That day's high temperature of roughly 36°C was 1°C shy of the heat wave alert threshold for coastal cities set by national meteorological authorities. But the effects of the heat were amplified by humidity — an often neglected factor in heat alert systems — and the lack of shade at the late-morning outdoor ceremony.

To help improve HAPs, urban planner Rajashree Kotharkar's team is working on a model plan that outlines best practices and could be adapted to local conditions. Among other things, she says, all cities should create a vulnerability map to help focus responses on the populations most at risk.

Such mapping doesn't need to be complex, Kotharkar says. "A useful map can be created by looking at even a few key parameters." For example, neighborhoods with a large elderly population or informal dwellings that cope poorly with heat could get special warnings or be bolstered with cooling centers. The Nagpur project has already created a risk and vulnerability map, which enabled Kotharkar to tell officials which neighborhoods to focus on in the event of a heat wave this summer.

HAPs shouldn't just include short-term emergency responses, researchers say, but also recommend medium- to long-term measures that could make communities cooler. In Nagpur, for example, Kotharkar's team has been able to advise city officials about where to plant trees to provide shade. HAPs could also guide efforts to retrofit homes or modify building regulations. "Reducing deaths in an emergency is a good target to have, but it's the lowest target," says climate researcher Chandni Singh.

reading.label: 2025 · Text 4
paragraphs: Navigating beyond the organised pavements and parks of our urban spaces, desire paths are the unofficial footprints of a community, revealing the unspoken preferences, shared shortcuts and collective choices of humans. Often appearing as trodden dirt tracks through otherwise neat green spaces, these routes of collective disobedience cut corners, bisect lawns and cross hills, representing the natural capability of people (and animals) to go from point A to point B most effectively.

Urban planners interpret desire paths as more than just convenient shortcuts; they offer valuable insights into the dynamics between planning and behaviour. Ohio State University allowed its students to navigate the Oval, a lawn in the centre of campus, freely, then proceeded to pave the desire paths, creating a web of effective routes students had established.

Yet, reluctance persists among other planners to integrate desire paths into formal plans, citing concerns about safety, environmental impact, or primarily, aesthetics. A Reddit webpage devoted to the phenomenon, boasting nearly 50,000 members, showcases images of local desire paths adorned with signs instructing pedestrians to adhere to designated walkways, underscoring the rebellious nature inherent in these human-made tracks. This clash highlights an ongoing struggle between the organic, user-driven evolution of public spaces and the desire for a visually curated and controlled urban environment.

The Wickquasgeck Trail is an example of a historical desire path, created by Native Americans to cross the forests of Manhattan and move between settlements quickly. This trail, when Dutch colonists arrived, was widened and made into one of the main trade roads across the island, known at the time as de Heere Straat, or Gentlemen's Street. Following the British assumption of control in New York, the street was renamed Broadway. Notably, Broadway stands out as one of the few areas in NYC that defies the grid-based system applied to the rest of the city, cutting a diagonal across parts of the city.

In online spaces, desire paths have sparked a fascination that can approach obsession, with the Reddit page serving as a hub. Contributors offer a wide array of stories, from little-known new shortcuts to long-established alternate routes.

Animal desire paths, such as ducks forging trails through frozen ponds or dogs carving direct routes in gardens, highlight the adaptability of these trails in both human and animal experiences. As desire paths criss-cross through both physical and virtual landscapes, they stand as a proof of the collective insistence on forging unconventional routes and embracing the spirit of communal choice.

newtype.passage:
Five Steps to Suggesting a Change at Work That’ll Actually Get Taken Seriously

Everyone wants to be that person—the one who looks at the same information as everyone else, but who sees a fresh, innovative solution. However, it takes more than simply having a good idea. How you share it is as important as the suggestion itself. Why? Because writing a new script—literally or figuratively—means that other team members will have to adapt to something new. Not to mention, if the process you're scrapping is one someone else suggested, there's the possibility of hurt feelings. To gain buy-in on an innovative, new idea, follow these steps:

items.text: Great ideas don't stand alone. In other words, you can't mention your suggestion once and expect it to be adopted. To see a change, you'll need to champion your plan and sell its merits. In addition, you need to be willing to stand up to scrutiny and criticism and be prepared to explain your innovation in different ways for various audiences.

Sometimes it makes sense to go to your boss first. But other times, it's useful to build a coalition among your co-workers or other stakeholders. When it works, it works great—because you're ready for your stubborn supervisor's pushback with answers like, "Actually, I connected with a few people in our tech department to discuss how much time these kinds of website updates would take, and they suggested they have the bandwidth." However, just be certain you can explain your end-around approach as one that built your case, rather than simply circumvented your manager. The last thing you want is for your boss to feel embarrassed he wasn’t informed—which could lead him to quash the idea before it even takes off.

One of the biggest barriers to gaining buy-in occurs when the owner of an idea is viewed as argumentative, defensive, or close-minded. Because, let's be honest: No one likes a know-it-all. So, if people disagree with you, don't be indignant. Instead, listen to their concerns fully, try to understand their perspective, and include their concerns (and possible remedies) in future discussions. So, instead of saying, "Martha, our current slogan is confusing and should be updated," you could try, "Martha raises a great point that our current slogan has a long history for our stakeholders, but I wonder if we might be able to brainstorm a tagline that could build on that—and be clearer for new customers."

New ideas are the grandchildren of old ones. In other words, don't throw old solutions under the bus to make your improvement stand out. Remember that in light of whatever the problem the old system solved—or, maybe, has failed to solve in recent memory—it was a great idea at the time. Appreciating the older contributions as you suggest future innovations helps bolster the credibility of your idea.

When pitching a new idea, it's important to use the language of abundance instead of the language of deficit. Instead of saying what is wrong, broken, or suboptimal, talk about what is right, fixable, or ideal. For example, try, "I can see lots of applications for this new approach" rather than, "This innovation is the only way." Be optimistic but realistic, and you will stand out.

translation.source:
You know the moment—the conversation slows, then there's a pause. It's awkward, and so awkward that some people will panic and say anything. Do we all find such silences so stressful?

Researchers analysed the frequency and impact of gaps greater than 2 seconds during conversations, including an overview of previous studies which indicate that the fear of awkward silences can be so extreme that people avoid talking to strangers, even though doing so is likely to be an enjoyable experience.

During conversations with short gaps, people feel more connected to their conversation partners. But such feelings of connection markedly dip when entering a long gap. Long gaps between strangers are likely to be followed by a change in topic.

But the opposite seems to be true for conversations between friends. Long gaps there saw increased connection. Between friends, longer gaps seem to provide natural moments for reflection and expression.
translation.reference:
你知道那一刻——对话慢了下来，然后出现了停顿。这很尴尬，尴尬到有些人会惊慌失措，说出任何话来。我们所有人都觉得这样的沉默如此有压力吗？

研究人员分析了对话中超过2秒的停顿的频率和影响，包括对先前研究的概述，这些研究表明对尴尬沉默的恐惧可能非常强烈，以至于人们避免与陌生人交谈，尽管这样做很可能会是一次愉快的体验。

在对话中，短暂的停顿让人们感觉与对话伙伴更加亲近。但当进入长时间的停顿时，这种连接感会显著下降。陌生人之间的长时间停顿可能会由话题的转变而改变。

但对于朋友之间的对话来说，情况似乎正好相反。在朋友之间，长时间的停顿反而增加了连接感。在朋友之间，更长的停顿似乎提供了自然的反思和表达时刻。

Write your answer in about 100 words on the ANSWER SHEET. Do not use your own name in your email; use “Li Ming” instead. (10 points)
writing.partB: 48. Directions: Write an essay based on the chart below. In your essay, you should 1) describe and interpret the chart, and 2) give your comments. Write your answer in about 150 words on the ANSWER SHEET. (15 points)

A.why: 错在把真实困难当错觉。开头说求助困难有许多可理解原因，下文逐项解释，并未把这种困难说成虚幻现象。
A.m: n. 幻影, 错觉, 幻想

B.why: 错在把研究对象换成讨论活动。this回指为什么难求助的问题，而不是前面已经展开的一场讨论。
B.m: n. 讨论

C.why: 错在没有代际习俗。文章谈个人担忧和心理机制，没有把不求助解释为一项世代沿袭的传统。
C.m: n. 传说, 传统, 交付

D.why: 正确。this question回指首句为什么需要帮助时仍难开口，是心理学家长期感兴趣的研究问题。
D.m: n. 问题, 询问；v. 询问, 审问, 怀疑

1.cn: 心理学家几十年来一直关注人们为何难以开口求助这个问题。

A.why: 正确。reluctance to ask for help与前面的find it difficult to ask for help呼应，指不愿或难以开口的倾向。
A.m: n. 不情愿, 勉强

B.why: 错在雄心不是阻碍。has led to failures承接不求助的消极后果，不能说普遍渴望求助的雄心导致这些失败。
B.m: n. 野心, 志向

C.why: 错在缺少具体方向。tendency to ask for help会变成倾向求助，与全文讲难以求助及其失败后果相反。
C.m: n. 趋向, 倾向

D.why: 错在情绪方向相反。enthusiasm表示热衷求助，无法解释文章为何要帮助人们克服开口困难。
D.m: n. 巨大的热情, 热心

2.cn: 人们普遍不愿求助，甚至造成过引人注目的失败。

A.why: 错在与后续解释不对应。下文强调暴露弱点、担心显得无能，说明心理顾虑，不是注意力不足。
A.m: n. 注意, 注意力

B.why: 错在没有能力天赋要求。求助是沟通需要，原文未说必须具备特殊才能才可以向别人开口。
B.m: n. 天才, 才能, 有才干的人, 天资

C.why: 正确。courage由下文承认需要、暴露弱点和担忧无能具体说明，面对这些顾虑仍要开口需要勇气。
C.m: n. 勇气, 胆量

D.why: 错在没有等待过程。该段讲的是表达需要时的心理门槛，并未描述长期等待答复而需要耐心。
D.m: n. 耐性, 忍耐

3.cn: 开口求助需要勇气，因为这意味着承认自己有做不到的事。

A.why: 错在不是任何时候都如此的时间限定。后句重新表达前句承认有事做不到，没有谈动作何时发生。
A.m: 任何时候

B.why: 正确。In other words把communicating a need、something you can't do改说为broadcasting your weaknesses，是同义解释。
B.m: 换句话说

C.why: 错在并非强烈劝人行动。By all means常表示务必或当然可以，不能连接两个对同一心理处境的解释。
C.m: 尽一切办法, 一定

D.why: 错在两句没有相反意思。承认自己做不到与展示弱点是一回事，不应使用On the contrary制造对立。
D.m:
正相反
[法] 正相反, 相反地

4.cn: 换句话说，求助是在向别人展示自己的弱点。

A.why: 错在没有不切实际。承认自己有需要是实际发生的沟通行为，作者并不认为展示弱点本身不现实。
A.m: a. 不切实际的, 幻想的

B.why: 错在与诚实表达相反。前文是承认真实需要，未说求助者借弱点欺骗对方。
B.m: a. 迷惑的, 虚伪的, 欺诈的

C.why: 错在心理感受不匹配。tiresome偏令人厌烦，下句却谈担心无能、失控等不安，不是在说求助耗时乏味。
C.m: a. 累人的, 烦人的

D.why: 正确。uncomfortable概括暴露不足时的难堪和不安，随后以担心别人觉得自己无能来具体解释。
D.m: a. 不舒服的, 不自在的, 不安的

5.cn: 暴露自己的弱点可能使人感到不自在。

A.why: 错在顾虑的侧重。doubts也可指疑虑，但更侧重某事是否成立或可信的不确定；紧接take over和get credit，此处强调对未来失控后果的忧虑，concerns about更切合。
A.m: n. 怀疑, 疑虑( doubt的名词复数 ); 未确定；v. 怀疑, 疑惑( doubt的第三人称单数 )

B.why: 正确。concerns about losing control与后文take over、get credit相接，指害怕帮忙后控制权或功劳落到别人手里。
B.m: n. 关心, 忧虑

C.why: 错在不是提出改进建议。后文是求助者预想风险，并非给别人关于放弃控制权的建议。
C.m: suggestion（原形）：n. 提议, 意见

D.why: 错在没有隐私保密。该句涉及对协作后果的担心，不是有关于失去控制的秘密要守住。
D.m: secret（原形）：n. 秘密, 机密, 秘诀, 秘方；a. 秘密的, 极机密的, 隐蔽的, 暗中的, 神秘的, 偏僻的

6.cn: 你还可能担心，一旦有人来帮忙，自己会失去控制。

A.why: 正确。Once把开始帮忙作为后续风险出现的起点，后面perhaps表明这只是求助者的担心。
A.m: adv. 一次, 曾经, 一旦；conj. 一旦, 一经；n. 一次；a. 从前的

B.why: 错在条件方向相反。Unless会变成除非开始帮忙，否则就会接管；原文正是怕对方开始介入后接管。
B.m: conj. 除非；prep. 除...之外

C.why: 错在没有让步。有人开始帮助与可能接管并非先承认好处再作逆预期转折，此处需要设定风险发生的情景。
C.m: conj. 虽然, 尽管

D.why: 错在时间不合。Before会说成还没开始帮助就接管或得到功劳，偏离losing control的具体解释。
D.m: prep. 在...之前；conj. 在...之前；adv. 在前

7.cn: 一旦对方开始帮忙，也许就会接管事情，或拿走你先前努力的功劳。

A.why: 错在不是理论。担心成为nuisance是一种实际顾虑，并不是需要验证的抽象理论。
A.m: n. 理论, 学说, 原理, 意见, 推测

B.why: 错在不是从几项方案中选择。句子在继续列举不愿求助的原因，未给求助者一个可作选择的行动方案。
B.m: n. 选择, 精选品, 选择权；a. 精选的, 挑三拣四的, 上等的；该命令用于提示用户作出选择, 决定批处理文件的流程

C.why: 正确。another factor承接前面的无能感、失控担忧，继续添加影响求助意愿的因素。
C.m: n. 因素, 因数, 系数, 基因, 代理人

D.why: 错在语义层级。context是背景情境，后面的being a nuisance具体描述一种顾虑因素，而非整个求助情境。
D.m: n. 上下文, 背景, 来龙去脉；n. 上下文

8.cn: 另一个令人担忧的因素，是自己可能给别人添麻烦。

A.why: 错在没有称赞动作。being a nuisance与过度赞美不构成同类担忧，原文未谈夸奖对方。
A.m: overpraise（原形）：vt. 过度夸奖, 过奖；n. 过奖

B.why: 错在不是竞争。outperforming表示做得比别人好，不能解释为何向别人求助会给对方造成麻烦。
B.m: outperform（原形）：vt. 胜过；做得比……好

C.why: 错在不是重新评估对方。reassessing是再评价，而上下文关注请求帮助对他人时间和精力的打扰。
C.m: reassess（原形）：vt. 再评价, 再摊派, 再课税

D.why: 正确。inconveniencing the person与being a nuisance并列改说，都是担心求助会打扰别人。
D.m: inconvenience（原形）：n. 不便, 困难；vt. 使感不便, 使感困难

9.cn: 你可能害怕自己成了累赘，给寻求帮助的那个人带来不便。

A.why: 正确。reach out for help与全文反复的ask for help呼应，指向他人伸出求助之手、主动联系。
A.m: 开口求助

B.why: 错在不是定居或平静。settle down不能与for help表达联系别人求助，后文还在讲害怕请求被拒绝。
B.m: 使舒服地坐下, 定居, 平静下来, 专心于

C.why: 错在缺少移交对象。turn over通常需要说明把什么翻转或转交，不能直接替代向别人开口请求帮助。
C.m:
打翻, 营业额达到, 周转, 移交给, 翻阅, 反复考虑, 翻身
[法] 移交, 交付, 让渡

D.why: 错在不是回顾。look back指回想过去，后面的for help需要的是采取求助行动，而非回忆经历。
D.m:
回顾, 三心二意
[经] 银行对过去贷款的审查

10.cn: 自尊较弱的人可能尤其难以主动开口求助。

A.why: 正确。declining your request由下句such refusals直接复现，说明这里担心的是请求遭拒。
A.m: 拒绝， 谢绝

B.why: 错在没有引发拒绝感。considering只是考虑请求，不必然等于后文说的refusals。
B.m: consider（原形）：v. 考虑, 思考, 认为

C.why: 错在把批评与拒绝混同。criticising request是评价它不好，后文such refusals强调不答应提供帮助。
C.m: criticise（原形）：v. 批评, 吹毛求疵, 非难

D.why: 错在评估并不等于拒绝。evaluating只说衡量请求，无法直接承接下句把它视为遭拒的说法。
D.m: evaluate（原形）：vt. 评估, 评价, 赋值

11.cn: 你还会额外担心，对方可能拒绝你的请求。

A.why: 错在unnecessary表示不必要。拒绝令人担心的是关系状态不好，不是关系透露了不必要的信息。
A.m: a. 不必要的

B.why: 正确。negative about the status of your relationship指把拒绝看成关系不佳的信号，解释低自尊者为何更难求助。
B.m: adj. / n. 负面的；否定的；消极的；负数

C.why: 错在只说奇怪不足以对应焦虑。下文要求别把暂时无法帮忙针对个人化，担忧的核心是负面评价而非新奇陌生。
C.m: a. 奇怪的, 陌生的, 生疏的, 不熟悉的, 不可思议的, 外行的, 外地的, 异乡的

D.why: 错在没有方案是否可实行。impractical评价做法不现实，但本句说的是人际关系状态，观察对象不同。
D.m: a. 不切实际的, 不能实行的, 不现实的, 不合情理的

12.cn: 你可能把拒绝解读成双方关系存在某种负面问题。

A.why: 错在行动目标不足。后面的try to remind yourself是缓解求助障碍的办法，并不是再解释困难为何存在。
A.m: v. 解释, 说明

B.why: 错在前文已经识别了困难。此处要引出应对建议，identify只找出问题，不能体现减轻求助阻碍的目的。
B.m: vt. 识别, 认为...等同于, 确定, 使参与；vi. 一致, 认同

C.why: 错在时态与目的。difficulties已在前面发生并被列出，建议不是预测未来困难，而是处理它们。
C.m: v. 预测；预言

D.why: 正确。overcome these difficulties后接提醒人人需要帮助这一认知调整，说明怎样克服开口的心理阻碍。
D.m: vt. 战胜, 克服, 胜过；vi. 得胜

13.cn: 要克服这些困难，可以提醒自己：人人都有需要帮助的时候。

A.why: 错在否认与让步不合。否认自己显得无能不能直接解释为何接下来的研究是鼓励，作者承认的是人们的担心。
A.m: v. 否认；拒绝给予

B.why: 错在与前文反复焦虑相反。forget会说忘记显得无能这件事，但while需要承认仍可能有这种顾虑。
B.m: vt. 忘记, 忽略, 忘；vi. 忘记

C.why: 错在miss不表达这种担忧。coming across as incompetent是担心出现的印象，不是遗憾错过的机会。
C.m: n. 失误, 避免, 失败, 小姐；vt. 未得到, 未达到, 未听到, 未觉察, 逃脱, 遗漏, 错过, 思念；vi. 失败, 击不中

D.why: 正确。fear coming across as incompetent回扣前文worry，while再转向研究显示的相反评价。
D.m: n. 恐怖, 害怕, 担心；v. 害怕, 恐惧, 为...担心, 敬畏

14.cn: 虽然你可能害怕显得无能，但研究发现求建议者反而被认为更有能力。

A.why: 错在假扮带来虚假性。disguised as强调伪装成某身份，研究说的是别人怎样真实评价求助者。
A.m: disguise（原形）：n. 假面目, 假装；vt. 假装, 隐瞒

B.why: 正确。are perceived as more competent表示被他人认为更有能力，直接回应怕给人无能印象的顾虑。
B.m: v. 感觉( perceive的过去式和过去分词 ); 视为; 认为; 理解为

C.why: 错在followed as不能表达评价。followed表示被跟随，无法说明研究测得的能力印象。
C.m: a. 跟随的；服从的

D.why: 错在不是引荐。introduced as通常说被介绍为某身份，文中没有人把求助者介绍给别人，而是对其能力的看法。
D.m: introduce（原形）：vt. 介绍, 引入, 采用, 输入

15.cn: 研究显示，向人请教者被看作更有能力，而不是能力更差。

A.why: 正确。recall times they'd sought help in the past表示回想以往求助的时刻，与设计情景的研究方式并列。
A.m: n. 回忆, 召回, 撤消；vt. 回想, 回忆, 召回, 撤消, 使恢复

B.why: 错在没有分类维度。classify需要按类别整理经历，原文只要求被试想起既往求助事件。
B.m: vt. 分类, 归类, 分等

C.why: 错在添加深入分析任务。analyse可谈研究者分析数据，但此处asking people to后的被试任务是回忆过去经历。
C.m: vt. 分析, 细察, 分解

D.why: 错在缺少比较双方。句中没有把不同经历并列比较，只说调取曾经求助的记忆。
D.m: vt. 比较, 比喻, 对照；vi. 相比；n. 比较

16.cn: 研究既设计求助互动，也请人回忆过去寻求帮助的经历。

A.why: 错在勇敢并非研究指标。下句谈帮助者感觉良好，整段讨论意愿与感受，没有衡量助人是否勇敢。
A.m: a. 勇敢的, 美好的, 华丽的；n. 勇敢者；vt. 勇敢地面对

B.why: 错在情绪方向不合。后面说助人让人feel good且有满足感，并非别人对提供帮助感到失望。
B.m: a. 失望的

C.why: 正确。willing to help与how good it'll make the help-giver feel并列，说明求助者低估他人的意愿和积极感受。
C.m: a. 乐意的, 自愿的, 甘愿的

D.why: 错在与underestimate的鼓励含义相反。hesitant会变成低估别人的犹豫，反而劝人少求助，不合研究鼓励开口的结论。
D.m: a. 迟疑的, 踌躇的, 犹豫不定的

17.cn: 求助者通常低估了别人愿意帮助自己的程度。

A.why: 错在放松并非本句回报。助人可能耗精力，前文how good强调积极心理感受，而不是一定使人松弛。
A.m: relax（原形）：vi. 放松, 松懈, 松弛, 变从容, 休息, 休养；vt. 使松弛, 缓和, 使松懈, 使休息

B.why: 错在没有意外性。研究所述感受是助人带来的满足，未说帮助别人的机会出乎意料。
B.m: surprise（原形）：n. 惊奇, 奇袭, 诧异；vt. 使惊奇, 撞见, 奇袭

C.why: 正确。rewarding说明助人有积极心理回报，对应前面的how good it'll make the help-giver feel，并非一定有金钱报酬。
C.m: 有满足感

D.why: 错在与鼓励方向相反。demanding强调费力、要求高，括号这里用于解释帮助者为什么愿意帮且感觉好。
D.m: a. 要求高的, 费力的

18.cn: 对多数人来说，有机会帮助别人会带来满足感。

A.why: 错在因果连接不准确。后句是在已有建议之外增加对象时机的考虑，不是由助人感到满足直接推出的唯一结果。
A.m: adv. 如此, 因此, 到如此程度

B.why: 正确。Also补充另一条建议：既要记住人们更愿意帮助，也要照顾求助对象与时间是否合适。
B.m: adv. 也, 并且, 同样地

C.why: 错在没有依次列举的最后一步。这里不是first、then之后收束步骤，而是补充求助时仍应注意的条件。
C.m: adv. 最后, 终于

D.why: 错在会替换而非补充。Instead会变成不要记住研究、改为挑时机，但文章要求两方面同时考虑。
D.m: adv. 作为替代, 反而

19.cn: 下次求助时记住这些发现，同时也要留意向谁、何时求助。

A.why: 错在礼貌不是无法帮忙的原因。too polite不能自然解释对方为什么现在没有时间或能力提供帮助。
A.m: a. 有礼貌的, 文雅的, 客气的, 有教养的

B.why: 错在把拒绝归咎个人品格。too proud暗示对方骄傲，不合作者要求avoid taking it personally、寻找客观原因。
B.m: a. 骄傲的, 自大的, 自豪的, 辉煌的, 壮丽的

C.why: 正确。too busy提供时间上的客观解释，与后面的对能力没把握并列，说明不能帮忙未必针对你。
C.m: a. 忙碌的, 热闹的, 没空的；vt. 使忙；vi. 忙碌

D.why: 错在无懒惰证据。作者引导读者考虑忙碌或能力不确定，不能把一次无法帮忙直接推成对方懒惰。
D.m: a. 懒惰的, 怠惰的, 缓慢的；vi. 懒散

20.cn: 有人眼下帮不上忙，也许只是太忙，或对自己的帮助能力没有把握。

trans: 过去，美国消费者给那些他们认为主要靠小费维生的人小费，例如收入低于最低工资的餐厅服务员。
2010年代初，许多企业开始用iPad和其他数字支付系统处理交易。
这些系统经常提示顾客给此前没有小费惯例的服务支付小费。
如今索要小费常与过去决定何时、如何给小费的薪酬和服务惯例脱节。
过去顾客几乎总是在服务结束后给小费，例如吃完饭、理完发或披萨送达之后。
这种支付时机既能奖励优质服务，也能激励工作人员提供优质服务。
在服务之前就要求顾客给小费，变得越来越常见。
而新的小费技术甚至可能自动加收小费。
数字支付设备的普及，使向顾客索要小费变得更容易。
这有助于解释，为什么索要小费正逐渐扩展到新种类的服务。
如今顾客经常看到默认小费建议菜单，金额往往远超账单的20%。
小费比例从1950年代的10%或更低，升到2000年前后的15%，再升到如今的20%或更高。
这种上涨有时被称为“小费膨胀”，即对小费金额不断提高的预期。
小费一直是传统收小费行业工作人员的重要收入来源，例如餐饮业；这些岗位的最低时薪可能低至2.13美元。
小费扩张和小费膨胀，如今进一步补充了许多低薪服务人员的收入。
值得注意的是，小费主要使部分工作人员受益，例如服务员，却不能惠及厨师、洗碗工等其他人。
为保证所有员工薪酬公平，一些餐厅取消小费并提价，但这种无小费服务运动基本已告失败。
因此，为了不涨价也能提高员工收入，更多雇主正屈从于扩大索要小费、提高小费比例的诱惑。
不过，许多顾客感到沮丧，因为他们觉得索要小费过于频繁，金额也过高。
正如研究强调，如今给小费似乎更带强迫性、更少出于慷慨，且常与服务质量彻底脱节。
英国国民医疗服务体系建立时具有远见，提供高质量、及时的医疗，满足当时服务人群的主要需求。
近75年后，英国面临截然不同的健康挑战，这一模式显然已过时。
从预期寿命到癌症和婴儿死亡率，英国都落后于许多同类国家。
超过680万人等待就诊，无力支付私人医疗的人越来越难获得医疗服务；医疗成本还在挤压其他公共服务投资。
医疗需求继续增长，已接近极限的医护人员将承受更严重的压力。
应对医疗和照护危机的许多办法，早已被反复提出。
我们需要更擅长减少和分流医疗需求，而非仅仅管理需求。
需要向社区和初级医疗投入更多资源，减少对医院的依赖。
社会照护能力也应扩大，以支持人数不断增加的长期患病者。
尽管有二十年的战略规划和多项重大医疗改革，我们在这些目标上仍未取得实质进展。
这就是Reform智库发起“重塑健康”新项目的原因，该项目获十位前卫生部长支持。
我们共同呼吁更公开坦诚地讨论英国医疗的未来，并紧急反思现存的医院中心模式。
讨论必须从如何最大化国民健康开始，而非仅仅“修复”国民医疗服务体系。
例如，据估计，医疗本身仅解释约20%的健康结果。
更重要的是我们生活、工作和社交的地方，但政府间仍没有清晰战略改善这些社会健康决定因素。
更糟的是，国家肥胖防治战略等政策被废除后，纳税人还要承担治疗由此产生的糖尿病等疾病的高额成本。
Reform希望探讨医疗体系中的权力和资源应该如何分配。
哪些卫生职能应留在中央，哪些应交给常负责健康相关服务且更了解当地需求的地方领导者？
近几年，印度各地的高温行动计划不断增加。
一般而言，高温行动计划明确规定官员何时、如何发布高温预警并提醒医院等机构。
例如，那格浦尔的计划要求医院在夏天预留“降温病房”治疗中暑者，并建议建筑商在酷热天让建筑工人休息。
但政策研究中心的一份报告指出，现有高温行动计划实施情况参差不齐。
报告发现，许多计划缺乏足够资金。
这些计划的预警触发阈值，也常未按照当地气候定制。
在某些地区，单看白天高温就足以触发预警。
但在其他地方，夜间温度或湿度可能与白天最高温同样重要，都是判断风险的指标。
研究者说，孟买4月发生的中暑死亡凸显了更细致、本地化预警的必要性。
那天约36℃的最高温，比国家气象部门为沿海城市规定的热浪预警阈值低1℃。
但湿度和上午较晚举行的户外活动缺少遮阴，放大了高温影响；湿度却常被高温预警系统忽略。
为改进高温行动计划，城市规划师科特卡尔团队正在制定示范计划，概述最佳做法并可适应当地条件。
她说，所有城市都应绘制脆弱性地图，以把应对工作集中到风险最高的人群。
科特卡尔说，这种地图不必很复杂。
只需查看少数关键参数，就能绘制有用的地图。
例如，老年人口较多、或非正规住宅难以应对炎热的社区，可获特别预警或增设降温中心。
那格浦尔项目已绘制风险与脆弱性地图，使科特卡尔能够告诉官员，今夏出现热浪时该重点关注哪些社区。
研究者说，高温行动计划不应只包括短期应急响应，还应建议能使社区更凉爽的中长期措施。
例如，在那格浦尔，科特卡尔团队已能建议市政官员应在哪里种树来提供遮阴。
高温行动计划也能指导住房改造或建筑规范修订工作。
气候研究员辛格说：“减少紧急情况下的死亡是好目标，但那只是最低目标。”
跨出城市规划铺装道路和公园的“愿望小径”，是社区非正式的足迹，显露人们未说出口的偏好、共享的捷径和集体选择。
这些集体偏离规划的路线，常以绿地中的踩踏土路出现，抄近路、穿草坪、越山丘，体现人和动物尽量高效往返两点的能力。
城市规划者认为愿望小径不只是便捷的近路，它们还能帮助理解规划与行为的互动。
俄亥俄州立大学让学生自由穿行校园中央草坪，再将学生走出的有效路线铺成正式道路。
不过，其他规划者仍不愿把愿望小径纳入正式方案，理由包括安全、环境影响，尤其是美观。
一个拥有近五万成员、专门讨论愿望小径的Reddit页面，展示了带有要求行人走指定道路标牌的小径图片，凸显这些人行小径的叛逆性。
这一冲突凸显了公共空间由用户自然演化，与追求视觉上精心设计和受控环境之间的持续拉扯。
威克夸斯盖克步道是历史性愿望小径的一例，由原住民开辟，用于穿越曼哈顿森林、在聚落间快速通行。
荷兰殖民者到来后，这条小径被拓宽为岛上一条主要商路，当时称为绅士街。
英国接管纽约后，这条街被更名为百老汇。
值得注意的是，百老汇是纽约少数不遵循城市其余地区网格布局的地方之一，斜穿部分城区。
在网络空间，愿望小径引发了近乎痴迷的兴趣，Reddit页面成为讨论中心。
投稿者提供各类故事，从鲜为人知的新捷径到长期存在的替代路线。
动物走出的愿望小径，例如鸭子穿过结冰池塘、狗在花园走直路，体现了这类路线在人与动物活动中的适应性。
愿望小径纵横于现实和虚拟空间，证明人们共同坚持开辟非常规路线、拥抱社区集体选择的精神。

blocks.text: Five Steps to Suggesting a Change at Work That’ll Actually Get Taken Seriously
blocks.label: 标题

blocks.text: Everyone wants to be that person—the one who looks at the same information as everyone else, but who sees a fresh, innovative solution. However, it takes more than simply having a good idea. How you share it is as important as the suggestion itself. Why? Because writing a new script—literally or figuratively—means that other team members will have to adapt to something new. Not to mention, if the process you're scrapping is one someone else suggested, there's the possibility of hurt feelings. To gain buy-in on an innovative, new idea, follow these steps:
blocks.label: 导读

blocks.text: Great ideas don't stand alone. In other words, you can't mention your suggestion once and expect it to be adopted. To see a change, you'll need to champion your plan and sell its merits. In addition, you need to be willing to stand up to scrutiny and criticism and be prepared to explain your innovation in different ways for various audiences.
blocks.label: 本段

blocks.text: Sometimes it makes sense to go to your boss first. But other times, it's useful to build a coalition among your co-workers or other stakeholders. When it works, it works great—because you're ready for your stubborn supervisor's pushback with answers like, "Actually, I connected with a few people in our tech department to discuss how much time these kinds of website updates would take, and they suggested they have the bandwidth." However, just be certain you can explain your end-around approach as one that built your case, rather than simply circumvented your manager. The last thing you want is for your boss to feel embarrassed he wasn’t informed—which could lead him to quash the idea before it even takes off.
blocks.label: 本段

blocks.text: One of the biggest barriers to gaining buy-in occurs when the owner of an idea is viewed as argumentative, defensive, or close-minded. Because, let's be honest: No one likes a know-it-all. So, if people disagree with you, don't be indignant. Instead, listen to their concerns fully, try to understand their perspective, and include their concerns (and possible remedies) in future discussions. So, instead of saying, "Martha, our current slogan is confusing and should be updated," you could try, "Martha raises a great point that our current slogan has a long history for our stakeholders, but I wonder if we might be able to brainstorm a tagline that could build on that—and be clearer for new customers."
blocks.label: 本段

blocks.text: New ideas are the grandchildren of old ones. In other words, don't throw old solutions under the bus to make your improvement stand out. Remember that in light of whatever the problem the old system solved—or, maybe, has failed to solve in recent memory—it was a great idea at the time. Appreciating the older contributions as you suggest future innovations helps bolster the credibility of your idea.
blocks.label: 本段

blocks.text: When pitching a new idea, it's important to use the language of abundance instead of the language of deficit. Instead of saying what is wrong, broken, or suboptimal, talk about what is right, fixable, or ideal. For example, try, "I can see lots of applications for this new approach" rather than, "This innovation is the only way." Be optimistic but realistic, and you will stand out.
blocks.label: 本段

41.evidence: champion your plan and sell its merits；explain … for various audiences
41.why: 本段说好想法不会自行获采纳，要持续为方案争取支持、推介优点，并向不同受众解释；F的推销员角色统摄这些行动。

A.why: 本段着重反复推介优点、争取采纳及应对审视，不是把消极措辞改成积极表达；后者属于第45题的语言建议。

B.cn: 尊重过去的做法与贡献
B.why: 没有讨论旧系统及其历史贡献。本段关注新方案如何被别人认识和接受，尊重前人是第44题的重点。

C.why: 没有比较先找老板还是先联系同事的沟通路径；这里无论面对谁，都要推介价值并准备解释。

D.why: 不能把mention once不够理解成只要等待。本段要求主动champion和sell，而非让时间自行带来改变。

E.why: 接受审视与批评只是推介时应有的准备，不等于主动邀请反对；段落主线是持续争取支持和讲清优点。

F.cn: 像推销员一样推介方案
F.why: sell its merits直接对应推销方案价值，champion与面对不同受众解释也都属于主动推介工作。

G.why: 本段没有要求降低自我姿态或避免自以为是，而是要求主动捍卫方案、解释创新的价值。

42.evidence: go to your boss first；build a coalition … explain your end-around approach
42.why: 整段讨论先找老板或先争取同事支持的不同路径，并提醒不能让老板觉得被绕开；C概括选择和使用沟通渠道。

A.why: 语气是否积极不是本段焦点。案例强调先与技术部门沟通、取得事实支持，以及再向主管说明路径。

B.cn: 尊重过去的做法与贡献
B.why: 没有评价旧流程的历史贡献。段落讨论在组织中找谁、先后如何联系，不是新旧方案的功劳分配。

C.why: 先向老板提出、或先组建支持联盟，两种路线均需妥善解释，正是善用沟通渠道。

D.why: 没有要求延迟或耐心等待。段落给的是主动选择接洽对象、准备支持依据的办法，而不是时间安排。

E.why: supervisor's pushback是要准备回应的风险，不是号召主动招来反对；主线仍是建立支持和告知主管。

F.cn: 像推销员一样推介方案
F.why: 本段不以宣传优点为中心，而以找老板、同事和利益相关方的先后路径为中心，推销方案不能覆盖这一组织关系。

G.why: 不要让老板难堪是路径使用的边界，但段落未围绕自以为是或谦逊聆听展开，不能只抓这一个提醒。

43.evidence: No one likes a know-it-all；listen to their concerns fully；include their concerns
43.why: 作者反对争辩、防御与封闭心态，要求认真听取异议并纳入后续讨论，例子也先承认对方有道理；G概括谦逊态度。

A.why: 不能只把别生气归为乐观。段落核心是别自以为是、倾听并吸收异议，积极措辞的系统建议在第45题。

B.cn: 尊重过去的做法与贡献
B.why: 例子虽提旧口号有历史，但用来示范认可Martha的看法、吸收顾虑；本段总体针对谦逊开放的交流态度。

C.why: 本段不选择通过老板或同事哪条渠道，只讨论面对不同意见时怎样回应和修改自己的表达。

D.why: 段落没有让人等一等，要求的是听完整个顾虑并在以后的讨论中纳入，等待本身不能解决自以为是。

E.why: 认真处理已经出现的不同意见，不等于主动邀请阻力。作者先批评know-it-all，最后示范承认对方道理，主线是谦逊。

F.cn: 像推销员一样推介方案
F.why: 本段强调倾听和吸收对方顾虑，不以推介方案优势为中心；推介方案是第41题的主线，不能覆盖此处谦逊开放的态度。

G.why: 反对know-it-all、听懂对方观点并承认其合理性，都是降低自我中心、保持谦逊的具体做法。

44.evidence: don't throw old solutions under the bus；Appreciating the older contributions
44.why: 本段要求提出创新时不要贬损旧方案，要承认它当时的价值和前人的贡献；B直接概括尊重过去。

A.why: 积极评价虽有联系，但本段专门讨论旧方案与前人贡献，不是第45题那种全面改用积极措辞的建议。

B.cn: 尊重过去的做法与贡献
B.why: old solutions、a great idea at the time与older contributions反复出现，明确要求尊重过去的方案与贡献。

C.why: 段落不涉及找主管或联络部门等渠道，而是怎样评价已有制度和提出过它的人。

D.why: at the time是在承认旧方案当年的价值，不是说创新推广应多等一段时间，时间表达所承担的作用不同。

E.why: 文中没有要求引来反对者或征集阻力，重点是避免为了突出新方案就牺牲旧方案的声誉。

F.cn: 像推销员一样推介方案
F.why: 虽然末句说尊重前人会增加新想法可信度，具体办法仍是肯定旧贡献，而不是以推介优点覆盖整段。

G.why: 保持谦逊过于宽泛；本段围绕新旧关系和历史贡献展开，区别于上一段对待异议时的个人交流姿态。

45.evidence: language of abundance instead of … deficit；Be optimistic but realistic
45.why: 本段对照消极缺陷语言与积极可能性语言，要求强调可行与理想之处，并保持乐观而现实；A概括正面表达。

A.why: 从不只说wrong、broken转向right、fixable、ideal，并明说Be optimistic，整体是保持积极态度和表达。

B.cn: 尊重过去的做法与贡献
B.why: 没有回顾旧方案当年的贡献；这里对比的是建议中的负面与正面措辞，不是过去与未来的关系。

C.why: 没有讨论先与哪个部门或领导沟通。无论采用哪条渠道，作者都要求使用积极但现实的语言。

D.why: 段落没有推迟采纳或等待成熟的要求；建议着眼于当下怎样描述新想法的可能性。

E.why: 本段讨论积极而现实的措辞，建议强调可行性与可能性；没有主张主动征询反对意见，不能用欢迎异议概括其语言原则。

F.cn: 像推销员一样推介方案
F.why: 推介新点子只是场景，本段的特定方法是改用积极措辞；不宜用一般推销行为取代明确的情绪与语言原则。

G.why: 避免说only way有谦逊意味，但其与right、fixable、ideal及optimistic共同服务于正面表达，不是专论听取他人异议。

sentences.text: You know the moment—the conversation slows, then there's a pause.
It's awkward, and so awkward that some people will panic and say anything.
Do we all find such silences so stressful?

Researchers analysed the frequency and impact of gaps greater than 2 seconds during conversations, including an overview of previous studies which indicate that the fear of awkward silences can be so extreme that people avoid talking to strangers, even though doing so is likely to be an enjoyable experience.
During conversations with short gaps, people feel more connected to their conversation partners.
But such feelings of connection markedly dip when entering a long gap.
Long gaps between strangers are likely to be followed by a change in topic.
But the opposite seems to be true for conversations between friends.
Long gaps there saw increased connection.
Between friends, longer gaps seem to provide natural moments for reflection and expression.

2025.reference:
你知道那一刻——对话慢了下来，然后出现了停顿。这很尴尬，尴尬到有些人会惊慌失措，说出任何话来。我们所有人都觉得这样的沉默如此有压力吗？

研究人员分析了对话中超过2秒的停顿的频率和影响，包括对先前研究的概述，这些研究表明对尴尬沉默的恐惧可能非常强烈，以至于人们避免与陌生人交谈，尽管这样做很可能会是一次愉快的体验。

在对话中，短暂的停顿让人们感觉与对话伙伴更加亲近。但当进入长时间的停顿时，这种连接感会显著下降。陌生人之间的长时间停顿可能会由话题的转变而改变。

但对于朋友之间的对话来说，情况似乎正好相反。在朋友之间，长时间的停顿反而增加了连接感。在朋友之间，更长的停顿似乎提供了自然的反思和表达时刻。
